Why-provenance is the witness basis: for each valuation of the query that produces the value, the part of the source the query's patterns matched, one witness per derivation. Where-provenance is the location in the source a value was copied from. For a hierarchical data model and a query language that covers positive (SPJU) relational queries, the witness basis is preserved by the paper's query rewriting, and the minimal witness basis is the same for equivalent queries with equality conditions, while where-provenance is not invariant over equivalent queries in general and is preserved by rewriting only for a restricted class it calls traceable. Proofs are omitted, and nothing covers negation, aggregation, updates or additions to the source. | Read |
| [NOTE-921](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-921.md) | Halevy — Answering queries using views: a survey | A survey that separates two problems of answering queries from stored views: finding an equivalent rewriting, which query optimization needs, and finding a maximally-contained rewriting or all certain answers, which data integration needs when sources are incomplete. Its theoretical findings, mostly reported from other papers: an equivalent conjunctive rewriting exists only if one exists no longer than the query, so finding one is NP-complete in the size of the query and view definitions, and checking a candidate is itself NP-complete; the inverse-rules algorithm builds the maximally-contained rewriting, as a possibly recursive datalog program, in time polynomial in the query and views; and finding all certain answers is polynomial in the size of the stored data in many open-world cases, but co-NP-hard in that size under the closed-world assumption even for conjunctive views and queries, or open-world with union in the views or ≠ in the query. Choosing which views to store is left as the next problem; cost-based choice among rewritings is described for practical optimizers, without guarantees. | Read |
| [NOTE-922](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-922.md) | Olston & Widom — Offering a precision-performance tradeoff for aggregation queries over replicated data | Olston and Widom propose TRAPP: caches hold, for each numeric value, an interval its source guarantees to contain the current value, the source pushing a refresh whenever the value leaves it. A query carries a precision constraint R, and the system chooses which values to fetch exactly so that the answer interval is at most R wide whatever the true values, at least total refresh cost. For SUM (and AVG without a predicate) that choice is a 0/1 knapsack problem, NP-complete in general and polynomial with equal costs; COUNT and MIN have simple rules. Staleness becomes bounded imprecision, never error, and the cost of the source-side upkeep that guarantees this, and of setting the bound widths, is outside the optimization. The one experiment is 90 stock prices with random costs. | Read |
| [NOTE-923](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-923.md) | Kleinberg — The small-world phenomenon: an algorithmic perspective | On an n × n lattice where each node also gets q long-range links drawn with probability proportional to d^(−r), short paths exist for r = 0, but no algorithm that sees only the links of nodes the message has visited finds them faster than about n^(2/3) steps in expectation. At r = 2 the greedy rule (pass to the contact nearest the target in lattice distance) delivers in O((log n)²) expected steps (proved for p = q = 1); for 0 ≤ r < 2 every such algorithm needs Ω(n^((2−r)/3)) and for r > 2 Ω(n^((r−2)/(r−1))). So efficient decentralized search depends on how the long-range links are distributed relative to the lattice, not on the links' existence or on the graph's diameter. The k-dimensional version (r = k) is stated without proof, and the model is a lattice with a known distance that every node can compute to the target. | Read |
| [NOTE-924](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-924.md) | Fagin, Lotem & Naor — Optimal aggregation algorithms for middleware | Given m lists of the same N objects, each sorted by one attribute's grade, and a monotone function combining the grades, the threshold algorithm (TA) reads the lists in parallel, random-accesses each newly seen object's other grades, and stops once k seen objects score at least the combined score of the last grades read. It is correct for every monotone combining function, needs constant buffers, and is instance optimal among correct algorithms that make no "wild guesses": on every database its cost is within a constant factor of any such algorithm's, the factor being m + m(m−1)c_R/c_S, which is best possible when the combining function is strict (conjunction-like). Without the no-wild-guesses restriction no algorithm is instance optimal, and the counterexample is a two-list conjunction whose target sits in the middle of both lists, which any algorithm must search linearly. Fagin's Algorithm's sublinear cost O(N^((m−1)/m) k^(1/m)) is cited from Fagin, not proved here, and holds only when the lists' orderings are probabilistically independent. The model prices queries over a given set of single-attribute sorted lists. It does not price building or keeping the lists, choosing an arrangement, or any computation beyond accesses. | Read |
| [NOTE-925](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-925.md) | Larsen & Nelson — optimality of the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma | For n, d ≥ 2 and lg^0.5001 n / √min{n, d} < ε < 1 there is an n-point set in R^d such that every map into R^m, linear or not, that keeps all squared distances within 1 ± ε needs m = Ω(ε⁻² lg(ε²n)), which is Ω(ε⁻² lg n) once ε > 1/min{n, d}^0.4999. So the Johnson–Lindenstrauss bound is optimal up to a constant, and the distributional lemma plus a union bound is the best route. The proof is an encoding argument over k-sparse point sets with k = ε⁻²/256, and the count it ends on is m = Ω(k lg(d/k)). | Read |
| [NOTE-926](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-926.md) | Achlioptas — database-friendly random projections | A random projection keeps all pairwise distances of n points within 1 ± ε with probability at least 1 − n^−β when k ≥ (4 + 2β)/(ε²/2 − ε³/3) · log n and the matrix entries are independent ±1, or √3 times {+1, 0, −1} with probabilities 1/6, 2/3, 1/6. This is the same k₀ as the best bound for Gaussian projections. The proof shows that every even moment of a unit vector's projection is at most that of the all-equal vector (1, …, 1)/√d, and that this vector's moments are at most the Gaussian ones. | Read |
| [NOTE-927](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-927.md) | Lee & Naor — extending Lipschitz functions via random metric partitions | A random partition of a metric space whose pieces are small and whose points are, on average, far from piece boundaries yields a "gentle" partition of unity, and averaging a Lipschitz map over it extends the map into any Banach space. This gives ae(X) ≤ C log n/log log n for every n-point metric space X (Theorem 1.10), improving Johnson, Lindenstrauss and Schechtman's C log n; ae(X) ≤ C log λ(X) for doubling X; ae ≤ C r² on K_r-minor-free graph metrics; e(ℓ₂ᵈ, Z) ≤ C√d; and, with the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma, eₙ(L₂, Z) ≤ C√(log n). For maps into Hilbert space it does not improve Johnson and Lindenstrauss's K√(log n), and it leaves √(log n) open. | Read |
| [NOTE-928](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-928.md) | Linial, London & Rabinovich — the geometry of graphs | Every n-point metric embeds in ℓ₂ with distortion O(log n) in O(log n) dimensions (Theorem 3.2(1), attributed to Bourgain). The paper reproves the distortion bound by a randomized Bourgain-style construction into ℓ_p^{O(log² n)}, and it gets the dimension from Johnson–Lindenstrauss. Every embedding of a constant-degree expander into ℓ_p, 1 ≤ p ≤ 2, of any dimension, has distortion Ω(log n) (Proposition 4.2), so the bound is tight. The lower bound comes from Leighton and Rao's flow–cut gap, and the same embeddings give an O(log k) max-flow/min-cut gap for k commodities. | Read |
| [NOTE-929](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-929.md) | Alon & Klartag — optimal compression of approximate inner products | Storing every inner product and squared distance of n points of norm at most 1 in R^k to additive error ε takes Θ(n log n/ε²) bits once k ≥ log n/ε², Θ(nk log(2 + log n/(ε²k))) for log n ≤ k ≤ log n/ε², and Θ(nk log(1/ε)) below, for 1/n^0.49 ≤ ε ≤ 0.1. Comparing these counts across dimensions shows that some n points in R^k cannot be mapped into fewer than Ω(min{k, log(2 + ε²n)/ε²}) dimensions with additive error ε, for every ε ≥ 2/√n. A bipartite version of the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma reaches O(log(2 + ε²n)/ε²) dimensions; the one-family version at that size is left open. | Read |
| [NOTE-930](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-930.md) v2 | Johnson & Lindenstrauss — extensions of Lipschitz mappings into a Hilbert space | Lemma 1: any n points in ℓ₂ⁿ map into ℓ₂ᵏ, k = [K(τ) log n], with ‖f‖_lip‖f⁻¹‖_lip ≤ (1+τ)/(1−τ), by a Haar-random rank-k orthogonal projection, with positive probability. The proof concentrates the norm of a projected unit vector about its median by Lévy's isoperimetric inequality and takes a union bound over the normalized differences of the points; K ≥ (10/τ)² suffices. The lemma is a tool for Theorem 1: Lipschitz maps from n-point subsets of any metric space into ℓ₂ extend to the whole space with Lipschitz constant at most C(log n)^{1/2} times the original. | Read |
| [NOTE-931](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-931.md) | Baraniuk, Davenport, DeVore & Wakin — a simple proof of the restricted isometry property | If an n × N random matrix satisfies the concentration inequality used in JL proofs, Pr(\|‖Φx‖² − ‖x‖²\| ≥ ε‖x‖²) ≤ 2e^{−n c₀(ε)}, then a union bound over a (12/δ)^k-point net on each of the C(N, k) ≤ (eN/k)^k coordinate k-subspaces, with a short bootstrapping step from net to subspace, gives the restricted isometry property for all k ≤ c₁n/log(N/k) with probability at least 1 − 2e^{−c₂n} (Theorem 5.2). Gaussian, ±1 and Achlioptas's sparse ensembles qualify with c₀(ε) = ε²/4 − ε³/6, and the same argument gives the property in any fixed orthonormal basis. | Read |
| [NOTE-932](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-932.md) | Dasgupta & Gupta — an elementary proof of the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma | For n points in ℝᵈ and 0 < ε < 1, a projection onto a random k-dimensional subspace, scaled by √(d/k), keeps every squared pairwise distance within a factor 1 ± ε with probability at least 1/n once k ≥ 4(ε²/2 − ε³/3)⁻¹ ln n. The proof bounds each tail of the squared length of a random unit vector's first k coordinates by Markov's inequality on an exponential of Gaussian squares, and then takes a union bound over the n(n−1)/2 pairs. | Read |
| [NOTE-933](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-933.md) | Donoho & Tanner — observed universality of phase transitions | For Gaussian matrices, ℓ1 minimization (and its nonnegative LP form) recovers a k-sparse vector from n random measurements in dimension N with probability tending to 1 below a curve ρ(δ; Q) in the plane δ = n/N, ρ = k/n, and to 0 above it; this was proved earlier and is restated here as Theorem 2.1. In 2,948,000 linear programs over eight non-Gaussian ensembles at N = 200, 400 and 1600, the 50% success points fall on the same curves, but exact finite-N agreement is rejected: the differences from the Gaussian decay as N^(-1/2), so the paper supports only an asymptotic ("weak") universality, as an observation, not a theorem. | Read |
| [NOTE-934](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-934.md) | Barnett, Barrett and Seth — Granger causality and transfer entropy are equivalent for Gaussian variables | For jointly Gaussian stationary processes X, Y and Z, Geweke's Granger causality F_{Y→X\|Z} = ln(\|Σ(X\|X⁻⊕Z⁻)\|/\|Σ(X\|X⁻⊕Y⁻⊕Z⁻)\|) equals twice the transfer entropy T_{Y→X\|Z}, for multivariate predictor, predictee and conditioning variables (Eq. 13). The proof: OLS residual covariance is the partial covariance Σ(X\|Y), and a Gaussian's conditional entropy is ½ln\|Σ(X\|Y)\| + ½n ln(2πe). The authors keep G-causality apart from physically instantiated causation. | Read |
| [NOTE-935](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-935.md) | Seth — Measuring autonomy and emergence via Granger causality | G-autonomy ga_{X\|E} is the log ratio of a variable's prediction-error variance without and with its own past, given external variables E. G-emergence ge_{M\|m} = ga_{M\|m}·(1/N)Σ gc_{mᵢ→M} makes a macro variable emergent to the extent that it is both autonomous from and Granger-caused by its micro variables. Validated in a predator–prey model and a boids model, where flocking shows high G-emergence and Granger causation from the flock's centre of mass to each boid. Seth says the measures are relative to the predictor and the variables included. | Read |
| [NOTE-936](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-936.md) | Williams and Beer — Nonnegative decomposition of multivariate information | Redundancy is I_min(S; A₁…A_k) = Σ_s p(s) min_i I(S = s; A_i), the expected minimum specific information. Restricted to antichains of sources and ordered by α ≼ β iff every source of β contains one of α, the collections form a lattice. The Möbius inverse of I_min on it gives partial-information atoms that are nonnegative (Theorem 5) and sum to I(S; R). Interaction information is synergy minus redundancy for three variables and a signed mixture for four, which explains its negativity and its +1 bit for both 3-parity and three copies. | Read |
| [NOTE-937](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-937.md) | Bertschinger, Rauh, Olbrich, Jost and Ay — Quantifying unique information | For a target X and sources Y, Z, the unique information of Y is UĨ(X : Y \ Z) = min over Q ∈ Δ_P of MI_Q(X : Y \| Z), where Δ_P is the set of joints with the same (X,Y) and (X,Z) marginals. If unique information should depend only on those marginals, this is an upper bound on any such measure, and the shared and synergistic information it implies are lower bounds. It is zero exactly when the other source is Blackwell-sufficient. The measures are non-negative, satisfy the bivariate PI axioms and the identity property, and are a convex programme, but are bivariate only. | Read |
| [NOTE-938](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-938.md) | Kraskov, Stögbauer and Grassberger — Estimating mutual information | Two k-nearest-neighbour estimators of mutual information, I⁽¹⁾ and I⁽²⁾ (Eqs. 8–9), from the Kozachenko–Leonenko entropy estimate (Eq. 20) taken at one length scale in the joint and marginal spaces, so that the biases largely cancel. The only approximation is a locally constant density. Numerically the systematic error scales with k/N and vanishes for independent variables, a conjecture without proof; the ordered Weinman exponential is the one case where the stronger form fails. Extensions to multi-information (Eqs. 23, 30). Conditional mutual information is not treated. | Read |
| [NOTE-939](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-939.md) | Massey — Causality, feedback and directed information | The textbook DMC, P(y^N\|x^N) = Π P(y_n\|x_n), is the DMC used without feedback; the right definition is P(y_n\|x^n y^{n−1}) = P(y_n\|x_n). Directed information I(X^N→Y^N) = Σ I(X^n; Y_n \| Y^{n−1}) is at most I(X^N;Y^N), equal without feedback (Theorem 1), and in a causal system bounds what the output says about the source (Theorem 3), so feedback cannot raise DMC capacity. Statistical dependence has no direction; directed information does. | Read |
| [NOTE-940](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-940.md) | Schreiber — Measuring information transfer | Defines transfer entropy T_{J→I} as the Kullback entropy between I's transition probabilities with and without J's past, at history lengths k for I and l for J (Eq. 4), which is the conditional mutual information I(i_{n+1}; j_n^{(l)} \| i_n^{(k)}). It is directional and ignores static correlation. A kernel estimator is proposed. Tent-map and Ulam-map lattices show it detecting the coupling direction where time-delayed mutual information fails; a heart–breath pair shows an asymmetry that the author says a common trigger could also explain. | Read |
| [NOTE-941](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-941.md) | Eichler and Didelez — Causal reasoning in graphical time series models | Defines the causal effect of intervening on one component of a stationary multivariate time series on another at a later time, and relates it to strong Granger noncausality through mixed graphs. Under Assumption 2.3 (an intervention independent of the system's past and of the other contemporaneous variables, and acting on the future only through the present), a missing Granger edge a → b means no effect on b at the next step, a ∉ an(b) means no effect at any horizon, and time-series back-door and front-door criteria identify effects from observational data. A present edge is only "potentially causal". | Read |
| [NOTE-942](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-942.md) | Williams and Beer — Generalized measures of information transfer | With the I_min partial information decomposition, transfer entropy T_{Y→X} = I(X_{t+1}; Y_t \| X_t) is the unique information of Y_t about X_{t+1} (state-independent transfer, SITE) plus the synergy of X_t and Y_t (state-dependent transfer, SDTE). SITE alone suffices for perfect open-loop controllability (Theorem 1). Time-delayed mutual information is SITE plus redundancy. Two-source transfer splits into unique, redundant and synergistic parts. On a sleep-apnoea recording, heart→breath transfer is all SDTE. | Read |
| [NOTE-943](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-943.md) | Lizier, Prokopenko and Zomaya — Local information transfer as a spatiotemporal filter | Transfer entropy is the expectation of a local transfer entropy, t_{Y→X}(n+1, k, l) = log p(x_{n+1} \| x⁽ᵏ⁾_n, y⁽ˡ⁾_n)/p(x_{n+1} \| x⁽ᵏ⁾_n), defined at every point and possibly negative. Apparent transfer entropy conditions on the destination's past; complete transfer entropy also on its other causal parents. On elementary cellular automata, with k ≥ 6 (rule 110) and k = 16, local transfer entropy highlights gliders and domain walls as the dominant information-transfer structures; k = 1 and local time-lagged mutual information do not. The averages carry none of this. | Read |
| [NOTE-944](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-944.md) v2 | Harder, Salge and Polani — A bivariate measure of redundant information | I_min gives 1 bit of redundancy to two independent bits copied into the target, because it compares amounts of specific information and not their direction in the space of distributions over the target. The paper adds an identity axiom, I∩((X,Y); X, Y) = I(X; Y), and defines a bivariate I_red: project each posterior p(z\|x) onto the convex hull of the other source's posteriors, count what survives, take the smaller direction. I_red satisfies all four axioms and gives a nonnegative PID. It agrees with I_min except where I_min overstates redundancy. | Read |
| [NOTE-945](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-945.md) | James, Barnett and Crutchfield — Information flows? A critique of transfer entropies | Information flow from X to Y is information in Y attributable solely to X's past. Transfer entropy is not it. For Y_t = X_{t−1} ⊕ Y_{t−1} it is 1 bit, but the bit is synergistic, carried by both pasts jointly (co-information −1). For Z_t = X_{t−1} ⊕ Y_{t−1} both transfer entropies are 0, and the causation entropies (conditional transfer entropies) are 1 bit each, again localizing a joint bit. By PID, transfer entropy is unique plus synergistic information; conditioning adds synergy, it does not only remove redundancy. | Read |
| [NOTE-946](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-946.md) | Ay and Polani — Information flows in causal networks | In a finite causal Bayesian network, X_B is causally independent of X_A imposing X_S if setting x_A after setting x_S leaves X_B's post-interventional distribution unchanged. For every model on a DAG this holds iff every directed path from A to B meets S (ud-separation, Theorem 2). Information flow I(X_A → X_B \| X̂_S) is conditional mutual information with interventional probabilities in place of observational ones, zero under causal independence. Examples show it can differ from conditional mutual information and from transfer entropy in either direction. Example 6's one bit holds at k = 1, by the reading's check. | Read |
| [NOTE-947](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-947.md) | Giarrocco & Averbeck — sensory and choice information flow between A1 and PFC | In 37 sessions of simultaneous recordings from A1 and dorsolateral PFC of two macaques reporting by bar release whether two tones came from the same side, cue-side information flowed A1 to PFC only (onset 120–147 ms), while choice information (release or hold) flowed first PFC to A1 (onset 315–365 ms after target) and then A1 to PFC (352–419 ms), both peaking near 500 ms, close to the bar release. The flow measure is a lagged regression on one-dimensional projections, so the result is correlational, within a trial, and does not separate the decision from the motor response. | Read |
| [NOTE-948](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-948.md) | Kübler & Birbaumer — BCI and extinction of goal-directed thinking in CLIS | Of 35 patients trained with EEG BCIs in Tübingen, degree of paralysis explained BCI performance (η² = .40) only because of the seven in the completely locked-in state, none of whom reached the 70% needed for yes/no communication; without them the relation vanished (η² = .12, n.s.). All seven were already in CLIS when training began. The authors propose, by analogy with the curarized rat, that lost perception of the contingency between a response and its consequences extinguishes goal-directed thinking, while "passive sensory information processing is intact", and predict that a contingency learned before CLIS and carried into it should prevent extinction. | Read |
| [NOTE-949](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-949.md) | Slovic — the construction of preference | A review, from an award address, of the preference-reversal literature. Normatively equivalent elicitation procedures (choice against pricing, choice against matching) give systematically different orderings, and about 90% of reversals violate procedure invariance rather than transitivity. Two mechanisms explain them: an attribute weighs more when it is compatible with the response scale, and the prominent attribute weighs more in choice than in matching. Slovic concludes that for important, complex and unfamiliar options preferences are constructed on the spot in elicitation. The evidence is about the response under each procedure; nothing in it tests whether a constructed preference persists or changes later judgements. | Read |
| [NOTE-950](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-950.md) | Ma & Kragel — map-like emotion knowledge in hippocampus and vmPFC | In fMRI of 29 people passively watching 14 emotional films, decoders trained on hippocampal patterns predicted an independent sample's consensus ratings of 13 emotion categories better than positions in a two-dimensional affective space, and vmPFC showed the reverse; patterns could also be decoded into the activity of a Tolman–Eichenbaum Machine that had learned a grid built from rating correlations by random walk, hippocampus favouring its small-scale conjunctive layer and vmPFC its large-scale structural layer. Effects are small (prediction–outcome correlations of about 0.04–0.10), and no learning in the participants was measured. | Read |
| [NOTE-951](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-951.md) | Chaudhary et al. — intracortical spelling in a completely locked-in patient | A man with ALS (born 1985), who had used an eye-movement BCI with an auditory speller until February 2019 and was judged completely locked-in from a few weeks before implantation in March 2019, was given two 64- channel arrays in left motor cortex. Attempted and imagined movements gave no usable signal; from day 86 he was given auditory feedback of firing rate, matched target tones from day 98, and from day 106 spelled with the same speller he had used before CLIS. Over days 106–462 he produced intelligible text on 44 of 107 days on which spelling was attempted, at about 1 character per minute. | Read |
| [NOTE-952](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-952.md) | Pattee — the physics of symbols | The epistemic cut is the separation of subject from object, symbol from referent, controller from controlled, which dynamical laws cannot describe without losing the function across it (von Neumann's regress). Measurement codes a rate-dependent dynamical state into quiescent symbols and control is its converse; both are executed by non-integrable (non-holonomic) constraints. The cut is epistemic, not ontological, and in life it arises first at the genotype–phenotype control interface: in Pattee's account control of construction came first, not measurement. | Read |
| [NOTE-953](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-953.md) | Sung, Rigotti & Lee — factorized goal and uncertainty codes in lateral PFC | A reanalysis of 20 people's fMRI from a 2014 two-stage Markov task with cued goals and block-wise transition noise. Goals and transition uncertainty are linearly decodable, weakly, from vlPFC, dlPFC and OFC, in a geometry whose nonlinear dichotomies decode worse than goal and linear ones ("factorized"), and a goal decoder trained under one noise level transfers to the other. Goal separability and transfer in lateral PFC correlate with choice flexibility and optimality across subjects; uncertainty separability does not. Unfitted model-free agents show a flexibility–stability trade-off that model-based agents and humans do not. | Read |
| [NOTE-954](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-954.md) | Powers, Clark & McFarland — General Feedback Theory, Part I | Builds a hierarchy of negative-feedback control systems in which each order perceives only the feedback signals of the order below and acts only by setting their references, which are replayed recordings of their own past perceptions. An "imagination connection" sends those references back into the higher system's perception, so that it can remember, plan "mentally", hallucinate and dream, under a "mixing control" the authors cannot specify ("We are open to suggestions", p. 20). An inherited N-system, driven by error in intrinsic physiological variables, reorganizes the network at random, forming new input functions as well as new outputs; an organization persists when the behaviour it produces lessens intrinsic error. | Read |
| [NOTE-955](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-955.md) | Fuchs, Mermin & Schack — an introduction to QBism | QBism in eight pages. Quantum states and all probabilities, 0 and 1 included, are an agent's personal judgements; a measurement is "any action an agent takes to elicit a set of possible experiences", and its outcome is the experience it elicits. The agent applies quantum mechanics to everything external to her, other agents and their reports included, and to nothing but her "own direct internal awareness of her own private experience". Locality follows because one agent's experiences are time-like separated; the Bell parameter λ is set outside physical science. No theorem or model: an interpretive essay. | Read |
| [NOTE-956](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-956.md) | Parr & Friston — attention or salience? | A short review that separates two things called attention: gain control, which weights currently available sensory data by their estimated precision, and salience, the expected information gain of an action (typically a saccade) that would acquire new data. It then ties them together: a saccade is driven by a prediction that a location will be sensed with high precision, so covert attention to a place biases an overt saccade there, which the authors read as support for the premotor theory. | Read |
| [NOTE-957](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-957.md) | Feldman & Lynch — self-generated validity | A theoretical paper, with no new data. When the belief, attitude or intention asked about is not already in memory, the question creates it, and the created answer is later retrieved as an input to other answers and to behaviour; when it is in memory, question order and format still decide which earlier answer is used. An earlier response is used for a later one if it is accessible and more diagnostic than other accessible inputs. Expertise, direct experience and trait involvement reduce the effects, because they supply judgements already formed and rehearsed. | Read |
| [NOTE-958](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-958.md) | Sandved-Smith et al. — computational phenomenology of mental action | A three-level discrete active-inference model in which attentional states set the precision of the perceptual likelihood and meta-awareness states set the precision of the attentional likelihood; mental action is a choice of 'stay' or 'switch' over attentional states, defined at the second level only, against a preference to observe oneself 'focused'. Simulations reproduce the cycle of focus, mind-wandering, noticing and refocusing, with longer mind-wandering under low meta-awareness. The stimuli are fixed by the generative process, so mental action changes only how strongly they update belief; the likelihoods themselves are not learned. | Read |
| [NOTE-959](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-959.md) | Powers, Clark & McFarland — General Feedback Theory, Part II | Names six orders of perception, from spinal loops through sensations, configurations, sequences and relationships to system concepts, with demonstrations whose reaction times lengthen with order (about 0.3 s at third order, 0.4–0.45 s at fourth). The N-system "merely alters the properties of a system, thus changing the transformations applied to existing information" (p. 37): reorganization is a change of perception, felt as insight, and a new perceptual organization can be vetoed by imagining its use. Consciousness is defined as a feedback function under N-system action. Conflict freezes a lower system at a virtual reference, and a system switched "entirely to the imagination-connection" is one of the ego's defences. | Read |
| [NOTE-960](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-960.md) | Friston et al. — action and behavior: a free-energy formulation | Existence is taken to require a low-entropy ensemble density; an ergodic assumption turns that entropy into time-averaged surprise, and because the setup stipulates that action is the only way an agent changes the hidden states it senses, action as well as perception must minimize a free-energy bound on surprise. Action enters nowhere in the generative model: it is a gradient descent that fulfils proprioceptive and visual predictions, and in simulations of eye, arm, mountain-car and Lorenz movements it cancels unexpected perturbations so they are not perceived. The paper fixes the model and re-samples the data, and answers the worry that this confirms a wrong model by appeal to existence: agents without the right priors cannot exist. | Read |
| [NOTE-961](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-961.md) | Bruno et al. — self-assessed well-being in chronic locked-in syndrome | Of 168 members of the French LIS association invited, 91 answered and 65 gave usable ratings: 47 (72%) rated their present life at or above the midpoint between their best period before LIS and their worst period ever (median +3), 18 (28%) below (median −4). Happiness was associated with longer time in LIS (OR 1.5 per year), recovered speech (OR 20.5) and absence of anxiety (OR 0.19). All had chronic LIS after a brainstem vascular accident, a median of 8 years earlier; 55% had recovered some speech and 70% some limb movement, and answers were given with a proxy's help. | Read |
| [NOTE-962](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-962.md) | Owen et al. — detecting awareness in the vegetative state | A 23-year-old woman who met the clinical criteria for the vegetative state five months after a traumatic brain injury, told in the scanner to imagine playing tennis or walking through her house, activated the supplementary motor area for the first and parahippocampal, posterior parietal and lateral premotor cortex for the second, as 12 healthy volunteers did. The authors take her compliance as "a clear act of intention" that "confirmed beyond any doubt" her awareness. No question was asked or answered. | Read |
| [NOTE-963](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-963.md) | Powers — Feedback: Beyond Behaviorism | A control system "will produce whatever output is required in order to achieve a constant sensed result" (p. 77), so behaviour is the control of input, not output, and stimulus-response laws follow from the environment once the controlled quantity is found. Above the lowest level a system's output is a reference level for the level below, so the hierarchy closes through lower systems down to muscle effort sensed kinesthetically; its top is a set of inherited intrinsic reference levels whose error drives reorganization. The paper says nothing about imagination: every loop it describes closes through the environment. | Read |
| [NOTE-964](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-964.md) | Monti et al. — willful modulation of brain activity in disorders of consciousness | Of 54 patients diagnosed vegetative (23) or minimally conscious (31), 5, all with traumatic injury, produced task-specific fMRI activity to motor and spatial imagery commands; 4 had been admitted as vegetative, and 2 of those showed no behavioural sign of awareness at the bedside even after the scans were known. One patient, Patient 23, answered five of six autobiographical yes/no questions correctly by choosing which imagery to perform, the investigators scoring blind; the sixth gave no signal. He was not one of the two behaviourally unresponsive patients: retesting found inconsistent signs of a minimally conscious state, but no bedside communication. | Read |
| [NOTE-965](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-965.md) | Rauh, Bertschinger, Olbrich and Jost — Reconsidering unique information | Theorem 2: no redundancy function on the Williams–Beer lattice satisfies symmetry, self-redundancy, monotonicity, non-negative atoms and the identity axiom. In XORCOPY (two independent bits, their XOR, and the target their joint copy) identity forces three 1-bit atoms {i}{jk} under a 2-bit total, so {12}{13}{23} ≤ −1. Bertschinger et al.'s bivariate measures cannot be extended to that lattice. Their unique information is monotone in each argument as expected; their shared and synergistic information violate left monotonicity. | Read |
| [NOTE-966](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-966.md) | Griffith and Koch — Quantifying synergistic mutual information | Synergy is the whole minus the union of its parts. S_VK = I(X_1…n : Y) − I_VK, where the union information I_VK is the least I*(X_1…n : Y) over joints that keep every source–target marginal. It sits between WholeMinusSum and S_max, which respectively subtract redundancy and count unique bits as synergy, and correlational importance measures something else. Versions 1–2 held that independent predictors share no information about the target; v6 withdraws it. For two predictors I_VK is Bertschinger et al.'s optimisation, so S_VK is their CI. | Read |
| [NOTE-967](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-967.md) | Griffith, Chong, James, Ellison and Crutchfield — Intersection information based on common randomness | The redundancy is the information about the target in the Gács–Körner common random variable of the sources, I_∧ = I(X_1 ∧ … ∧ X_n : Y): the largest I(Q : Y) for Q a function of every source. It is defined for any n, satisfies target monotonicity, which no earlier measure did, and lies below I_min. But it is zero whenever the sources have full support, so it fails identity and continuity, and its synergy goes negative. A zero-error variant satisfies identity in zero-error form and goes negative too. | Read |
| [NOTE-968](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-968.md) | Ince — Measuring multivariate redundant information with pointwise common change in surprisal | I_ccs measures redundancy as the expected local co-information over only those events where each source, the joint source and the overlap change the target's surprisal in the same direction, under the maximum-entropy joint matching source–target and joint-source marginals. Defined for any number of sources. It keeps symmetry, self-redundancy, subset equality and an independent-sources identity, and drops Harder et al.'s identity, monotonicity and non-negative atoms. A game-theoretic argument that unique information depends on the source–source marginal is offered against Bertschinger et al. | Read |
